KESTREL HILL NEUROLOGY, Neuromuscular Clinic
Yearly review, 08/16/2022

Re: Tyler Boucher, DOB 07/29/1991

Dear Doctor,

Mr. Boucher finished his 8 weeks of physical therapy last October and has kept up the home program, walking or cycling most days. Since January he has worked from home as a freelance graphic designer. Stairs and limb strength are about the same as last year, and the double vision still comes and goes. No trouble swallowing, no palpitations or faints, no change in hearing.
Medications: cetirizine as needed, fluticasone nasal spray, monthly allergen immunotherapy.

Examination unchanged: bilateral ptosis, limited eye movements in more than one direction, mild proximal limb weakness.

ECG today: sinus rhythm 64/min, PR 160 ms, QRS 88 ms, QTc 408 ms. Normal and unchanged.

Plan: continue the home exercise program. Review in a year with an ECG.

Sincerely,
Neurology, Kestrel Hill Neurology

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: short of breath

HPI: 31M with mitochondrial myopathy and pollen allergic rhinitis, here for the breathing (also overdue for his physical, missed in October). About 16 months of getting more winded. Now has to stop after two blocks on a walk. He had assumed it was his muscles and let it go, but it has kept getting worse while the leg and arm weakness has not really changed. No chest pain. No fever. No leg swelling, no orthopnea.
Work: freelance graphic designer from home since early 2022, so much less physical than construction.
Never smoker, no vaping. Alcohol 1-2 drinks a week. No pets.
Family: father died mid-40s of cirrhosis blamed on alcohol, pt recalls he was always short of breath.

Meds: cetirizine PRN, fluticasone nasal, monthly SCIT at allergy.
Allergies: tree/grass/weed pollen. NKDA.

VS: BP 109/72, HR 59, RR 16, T 36.9, SpO2 94% RA, wt 64.9 kg, BMI 20.2.
Gen: thin, comfortable at rest, speaking full sentences.
Eyes: mild bilateral ptosis, unchanged.
CV: RRR, no murmur, no JVD.
Lungs: mildly prolonged expiration, no wheeze or crackles.
Ext: no edema, no clubbing.
Neuro: mild proximal weakness unchanged from prior.

A/P:
1. Progressive exertional dyspnea, never smoker, prolonged expiratory phase, resting sat 94%. This looks like more than deconditioning or his myopathy. Pulmonology referral placed for full evaluation. CBC and BMP today.
2. Mitochondrial myopathy, stable exam. Neurology review 8/2022 with a normal ECG; keeps up the home exercise program as best he can.
3. Allergic rhinitis, on SCIT.
4. Physical: overdue, will fold preventive items into the next visit.
Return precautions for chest pain or breathing at rest.

documents.title: After Visit Summary
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Today: shortness of breath with walking.

Plan: referral to pulmonology (lung specialists), who will likely do breathing tests. Blood count and chemistry panel drawn today, results in the portal.

Call 911 or go to the ED for chest pain, trouble breathing at rest, or blue lips.

We still owe you a physical; we will catch up on that after the lung visit.

documents.title: Lab Results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Your blood count is normal (hemoglobin 15.0, no anemia to explain the breathlessness) and the chemistry panel is normal. Pulmonology appointment is 6/13.

reports.text:
Sugarloaf Pulmonary Associates imaging. PA and lateral chest.
Indication: progressive dyspnea, never smoker.
Findings: Both lungs are hyperlucent at the bases, lower lobes more than upper. Both hemidiaphragms are flattened. No focal consolidation, mass or nodule. No pleural effusion or pneumothorax. Cardiomediastinal silhouette normal in size. Osseous structures intact.
reports.conclusion: Bilateral lower-lobe hyperlucency with flattened diaphragms.

reports.text:
Pulmonary function laboratory: spirometry with lung volumes by plethysmography. Effort and reproducibility acceptable.
FEV1/FVC: 0.58 (reduced).
Total lung capacity: 122% predicted (increased).
Residual volume: 165% predicted (increased).
reports.conclusion: Airflow obstruction with increased total lung capacity and residual volume, consistent with hyperinflation and air trapping.

documents.title: Pulmonology Consultation
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
SUGARLOAF PULMONARY ASSOCIATES
New consultation, 06/13/2023

Patient: Tyler Boucher, 31 y/o M
Referring: PCP
Reason: progressive dyspnea

HPI: Mr. Boucher has had worsening shortness of breath for about 18 months and is now breathless with very little effort. He used to jog regularly at an easy pace; now two blocks of walking leave him winded. He occasionally feels a mild tightness in the chest. He denies chest pain, wheezing, cough or hemoptysis. He has never smoked.

PMH: mitochondrial myopathy (neurology, 2021); seasonal allergic rhinitis on subcutaneous immunotherapy.
PSH: tonsillectomy.
Meds: cetirizine 10 mg PRN, fluticasone nasal 2 sprays each nostril daily, monthly allergen immunotherapy.
Allergies: tree, grass and weed pollen; no drug allergies.
Family history: father died in his mid-40s of cirrhosis that was attributed to alcohol; the patient recalls his father having chronic breathing problems. Paternal grandmother with cirrhosis of unknown cause.
Social: freelance graphic designer, works from home. Never smoker. Drinks socially. No recreational drugs. No pets.

Exam:
Vital signs normal other than respiratory rate 22 and SpO2 94% on room air.
General: thin, mildly tachypneic at rest, no accessory muscle use.
Lungs: no crackles or wheeze; expiratory phase mildly prolonged; hyperresonant to percussion bilaterally.
Cardiac: regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, no murmur.
Extremities: no clubbing, no cyanosis, no edema.

Data:
- Labs today: ALT 64 U/L and AST 52 U/L, both mildly elevated. Remainder of hepatic panel normal.
- Chest x-ray: hyperlucency of both lower lobes with flattened diaphragms.
- PFTs: FEV1/FVC 0.58, reduced. TLC 122% predicted and RV 165% predicted, both increased.

Assessment: Never-smoker in his early 30s with obstruction, hyperinflation and air trapping, a lower-lobe predominant pattern on chest film, mildly abnormal transaminases, and a father with lung trouble and cirrhosis at a young age. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency needs to be excluded.

Plan: Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level and phenotype sent today. I will write with the results.

Pulmonology, Sugarloaf Pulmonary Associates
cc: PCP

documents.title: Pulmonology Results Letter
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
SUGARLOAF PULMONARY ASSOCIATES
06/27/2023

Re: Tyler Boucher, DOB 07/29/1991

Dear Doctor,

Further to my consultation of 06/13:

Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin: 28 mg/dL (low).
Phenotype: PiZZ.

Diagnosis: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, ZZ phenotype. The lower-lobe emphysema pattern on his chest x-ray and the airflow obstruction with air trapping on PFTs represent the lung disease of his alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. His mildly raised transaminases on 06/13 (ALT 64, AST 52) are noted.

Treatment:
1. Albuterol HFA 90 mcg per puff, 2 puffs every 4 to 6 hours as needed for breathlessness. Prescription sent to his pharmacy.
2. I recommend augmentation therapy with intravenous alpha-1 proteinase inhibitor (human), 60 mg/kg once weekly, which is 3,840 mg at his weight of 64 kg. We are submitting the Medicaid prior authorization through the specialty pharmacy; the infusions would be given at home by an infusion nurse.
3. I will see him yearly with spirometry, sooner if his breathing changes.

I called Tyler today with the results and the plan and answered his questions. In light of this result he wondered whether his father's illness was the same condition.

Sincerely,
Pulmonology, Sugarloaf Pulmonary Associates
cc: PCP

documents.title: Follow-up Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
F/U after pulmonology.

Sugarloaf Pulmonary letters 6/13 and 6/27 reviewed with patient:
- RR 22, SpO2 94% at their visit; prolonged expiration, hyperresonance.
- CXR: both lower lobes hyperlucent, flat diaphragms.
- PFTs: FEV1/FVC 0.58, TLC 122%, RV 165%.
- ALT 64, AST 52.
- AAT 28 mg/dL, PiZZ. Dx alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, the emphysema being its lung disease.
- Pulm plan: albuterol HFA 2 puffs q4-6h PRN, started 6/27; weekly IV alpha-1 proteinase inhibitor 60 mg/kg augmentation by home infusion, Medicaid PA submitted by pulm; yearly spirometry.

Tyler is taking it in stride. Breathing about the same as April, two blocks before he has to stop. Has used the albuterol a couple of times on longer walks. No cough. Working from home.

Family history updated today: his father's lung trouble and early death now read as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency with early-onset emphysema; died mid-40s of cirrhosis. Other family history unchanged (mother mitochondrial myopathy, maternal uncle schizophrenia, paternal grandmother cirrhosis unknown cause, maternal relatives with early hearing loss, identical twin brother healthy).

Meds: cetirizine PRN, fluticasone nasal, monthly SCIT, albuterol HFA PRN (pulm).
Allergies: tree/grass/weed pollen. NKDA.
Alcohol 1-2/wk. Never smoker.

VS: BP 106/67, HR 69, RR 17, T 36.7, SpO2 94% RA, wt 63.5 kg, BMI 19.8.
Gen: thin, NAD.
Lungs: mildly prolonged expiration, no wheeze.
CV: RRR.
Abd: soft, no HSM.
Eyes/neuro: mild ptosis and proximal weakness, unchanged.

A/P:
1. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ) with lower-lobe emphysema, new dx by pulm. Pneumococcal vaccine (PCV20) today for chronic lung disease. Hepatic panel today to follow the transaminases. Albuterol PRN per pulm; augmentation infusions to start once the PA is approved.
2. Mitochondrial myopathy: CK today as well, last one 612 in 2021. Neurology yearly review due next month.
3. Allergic rhinitis on SCIT.
4. Physical due in the fall.

KESTREL HILL NEUROLOGY, Neuromuscular Clinic
Yearly review, 08/15/2023

Re: Tyler Boucher, DOB 07/29/1991

Dear Doctor,

Since I last saw Mr. Boucher, pulmonology has diagnosed alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ) with emphysema, which accounts for the breathlessness he had put down to his muscles. He has an albuterol inhaler for as-needed use and his first weekly augmentation infusion is scheduled for this week. From the muscle side he is unchanged: stairs and limb strength as before, occasional double vision, no trouble swallowing, no palpitations or faints, no hearing change. He walks most days at a pace his breathing allows.

Examination unchanged: bilateral ptosis, limited eye movements in more than one direction, mild proximal limb weakness.

ECG today: sinus rhythm 66/min, PR 152 ms, QRS 92 ms, QTc 415 ms. Normal and unchanged.

Plan: continue the home exercise program within his breathing limits. Review in a year with an ECG.

Sincerely,
Neurology, Kestrel Hill Neurology
